data.title: US economists win Nobel for research helping policymakers navigate crises

data.title: Cyberattack hits hundreds of French supermarkets, spoiling millions of euros in food
data.description: Hundreds of supermarkets across France have been targeted in an unprecedented cyberattack that remotely altered the temperatures of fridges and freezers, causing large quantities of fresh and frozen food to spoil. Major retailers, including Carrefour, Monoprix, E.Leclerc and Coopérative U, were affected, with the Les Mousquetaires group reporting around 300 impacted stores. Losses could reach several million euros. The refrigeration systems involved used outdated software that no longer received security updates. Some fires were also reported, and French authorities have launched an investigation to identify those responsible.

data.title: ‘I knew I was being followed’: Keira Knightley on her hacking nightmare – and new Stasi spy play The Lives of Others
data.description: As the Oscar-winning Stasi surveillance film hits the stage, Knightley and co-star Luke Thompson talk about the paranoia at its heart, the cost of theatre tickets nowadays – and their fury at ringtones in the stalls Unpacking assorted tubs of carrot sticks and salad, Keira Knightley winces apologetically. “I just realised I’ve got very crunchy food,” she says. How apropos that she should consider the impact that her lunch might have on my audio recording when we are here to discuss The Lives of Others , a new play in which the characters are divided between the spies and the spied-upon. Based on the Oscar-winning 2006 film and set in East Berlin in 1984, the play stars Knightley as Christa-Maria, a theatre actor in a relationship with a director, Georg, played by Luke Thompson. Earwigging on them is Wiesler (Stephen Dillane), the Stasi officer whose principles are gradually challenged and weakened by his round-the-clock exposure to this cultured couple. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘Some things are worth dying for’: Karl Bushby’s incredible 28-year walk home, through deserts, kidnappers and polar bears
data.description: The ex-soldier has marched 36,000 miles since he left Hull in 1998. He’s crossed the Americas, Asia and Europe, fallen in love, been held at gunpoint and been deported, in between nearly drowning, nearly dying of thirst and nearly being eaten. But that’s just the start of it … ‘It’s a big moment,” says Karl Bushby, who has had plenty of big moments in his life. He is recording himself on his phone for social media. “We’re in Dover, and I’m about to have my first fish and chips and mushy peas in 28 years. Mushy peas, my God, I forgot they even existed!” He points his phone at the plate in front of him. “It better be good.” And he tucks in. “Mmmm. See, this is a big chunk of fish and a decent bit of batter, and that’s something you don’t see in other parts of the world. I mean, come on! That. Is. Fish. And. Chips! You see, Britain is special.” It has been two days since Bushby swam the Channel to return to England. Tomorrow, he’ll start the walk home to Hull for the first time since he left in 1998. He hopes to get back on 1 November, the same date he set off all those years ago. Continue reading...

data.title: Europe’s big election season is about to kick off. It could change everything | Nathalie Tocci
data.description: If far right nationalists gain power in four big countries simultaneously, we are in for a dramatic Trumpian tilt When it comes to Europe’s economy or its peace and security, it is obvious that decision-making has to be done largely at the European level to be meaningful. Yet electoral politics is still conducted mostly at the national level. The silver lining of this mismatch is that from country to country in Europe we have governments with different political priorities and leanings. Unlike in the US, where one presidential election can radically change the entire country’s course, as we have seen so vividly under Donald Trump’s leadership, the same drama has not so far unfolded in Europe. This may be about to change. Pedro Sánchez rolled the dice in Spain last week, calling a snap election for next month after an unholy alliance of the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox and Catalan pro-independence party Junts blocked his big housing reform package in parliament. If the socialist prime minister, hailed by progressives globally but demonised by Europe’s right and Trump’s US, loses his election gamble, Spain could fall into the hands of a conservative/far-right coalition, which is currently ahead in the polls. Nathalie Tocci is a Guardian Europe columnist Continue reading...

data.title: I was kidnapped and held hostage for 977 days. Could I forgive my captors?
data.description: At first the idea of mercy was something that helped me through the ordeal. But would real forgiveness be a form of Stockholm syndrome? I knew Mohamed Tahlil as a gentle pirate who oversaw a team of guards during the first months of my life as a hostage in 2012. I had travelled to Somalia to report on the outbreak of modern piracy off the coast. On the 10th day, along a dusty road near Galkayo, in the centre of the country, I was kidnapped by pirates. For the next two and a half years, I was a hostage. I spent most of my time on a thin, sweat-soaked foam mattress on the floor of a dusty room. The dim concrete prison houses changed, but the filth and the circumstances didn’t. Sometimes my captors moved me into the Somali savannah – where we camped in the open and slept on the ground – and for a six-month stretch, I was held on a hijacked tuna vessel, where I joined 28 fishers from east Asia who had been captured about three weeks before I was placed on board. (They had captured me on land, but they were a pirate gang, organised to capture ships at sea.) In each location, pirate guards would sit around with AK-47s and listen to the radio, or else chew khat, a narcotic plant. Continue reading...

data.title: Andy Burnham will take Britain back into European Union, Neil Kinnock claims – UK politics live
data.description: Former Labour leader says he believes the prime minister has an ‘authentic commitment’ to taking the UK back into the EU Andy Burnham promises ‘serious dialogue’ over UK’s relationship with EU Zia Yusuf , Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, has said he does not agree with his colleague Suella Braverman’s assertion that black people cannot be English. Asked about her views in an interview on Sky News , Yusuf said: In my view Ashley Cole is the best English fullback in history, and I won’t take any other position. So in my view, Ashley Cole is English. I think the argument that he’s not English doesn’t hold water with me. Nasser Hussain, who I grew up watching when I went to the cricket, the idea that those people aren’t English is an alien concept to me. I would respectfully disagree with people, who make the opposite argument. To say I’m English is to take a ‘laissez-faire, anything-goes’ attitude to ethnicity, citizenship and identity. It also denies me my Asian heritage. The liberals (many of them in today’s Conservative party) take this cosmopolitan approach to Englishness. They’re terrified of being called racist so they say that anyone, as long as they’re born here, can be English. I take the conservative approach. Englishness is an ethnicity. There have been English people for centuries and we need to recognise this more if we are to start taking a more muscular approach to citizenship and nationality. And no, it’s not racist to say this. Continue reading...

data.title: Bedbug infestation forces Qantas to ground plane in Rome
data.description: Aircraft taken out of operation after flight from Perth after the discovery of parasitic insects on board Qantas has been forced to ground a plane in Rome after bedbugs were discovered on the aircraft on its way from Perth. The parasitic insects were found in the front of the economy section of the Boeing 787 Dreamliner as it made its way from Perth to Rome for the QF5 flight on 9 October, a source with knowledge of the incident confirmed on Tuesday. data.description: Case of couple who wed legally in Austria exposes clash between EU court ruling and national restrictions A same-sex couple are suing authorities in Slovakia for refusing to register their Austrian marriage, testing whether a landmark EU court ruling can turn recognition abroad into legal security at home. Their fight exposes a clash between European obligations and national restrictions – and what that means for LGBTQ+ people living under Robert Fico’s populist-nationalist government. data.description: Cambridge University study suggests stark gender divide in misdiagnosis, with women also waiting longer for treatment Women with autoimmune conditions are up to 74% more likely than men to be told their symptoms are psychological or psychosomatic, and face much longer waits for a diagnosis and treatment, a study suggests. Hundreds of millions of people – about one in 10 globally – are affected by autoimmune conditions, which can cause a range of health issues including fatigue, muscle pain and rashes. data.title: RJ Mitte, actor best known for Breaking Bad, dies aged 34
data.description: Actor who played Walter White Jr on the acclaimed show and advocated for disability representation remembered by Bryan Cranston as ‘my sweet son’ RJ Mitte – a life in pictures The actor RJ Mitte, whose personal experience living with cerebral palsy informed his role as Walter White Jr in the television series Breaking Bad, has died aged 34 in Brownsville, Texas. “It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” Mitte’s representatives said in a statement. “Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion.” Continue reading...

data.title: Trill seekers: can scientists use AI and tutors to help birds remember lost songs?
data.description: When populations fall, fledglings can struggle to learn the right notes to attract mates. But research on how birds communicate offers hope for species’ survival Listening to birdsong is one of life’s great joys, but when researchers heard a particular tune emerging from a tree in a Buenos Aires park, they were especially jubilant. This arrangement was among those chirped by the local rufous-collared sparrows in the 1960s, but had since disappeared from the area. That was until scientists created a computer-generated rendition, curious to find out if birds might consider it realistic enough to imitate. Less than three months later, a local avian resident began to copy parts of the song. Continue reading...

data.title: AI godfather Geoffrey Hinton: ‘We’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans’
data.description: Pioneering computer scientist on why Trump is using ‘superintelligence’ wrong, whether AI could wipe out humanity – and how our biggest challenge will be accepting we’re not the only intelligent beings Donald Trump is a “corrupt, senile felon” whose fixation on the term superintelligence proves he knows nothing about AI , said Geoffrey Hinton , “godfather” of the technology, in a wide-ranging interview where he doubled down on recent warnings that AI models pose an existential threat to humanity and scoffed at claims the industry could regulate itself. The pioneering computer scientist, whose work helped lay the foundations of modern AI, has since become one of the technology’s most vocal critics. His latest remarks come after a tumultuous month during which a growing list of senior AI scientists and researchers have joined Hinton in ringing the alarm about how the technology he helped create could ultimately escape human control, sparking an industry crisis, the hasty assembly of congressional meetings and a rare global consensus that something must be done. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘Girls aren’t supposed to be cocky’: Sophia Stel on the pressure of writing The Greatest Album Of All Time
data.description: Raised as one of 11, the Vancouver artist (and model) is now signed by A24. She talks about her ultra-religious childhood and how – despite her album title – she still suffers from imposter syndrome The first time Sophia Stel came to London, she slept outside in the freezing cold. The Vancouver songwriter had finished a live set last autumn, then gone out until 3am with her then crush, but when they returned to their Airbnb, they found that Stel’s manager had dead-bolted the door and fallen asleep. Stel plus crush looked for a hotel but ultimately had no choice but to kip on the doorstep. “We hadn’t spent that much time together and I got to see how she was in a stressful situation,” Stel says, smiling at the memory. “She kept her vibe up and tried to solve it – I knew I was so in love then.” A lot has changed in Stel’s life in the year since. She opened her business bank account as an artist, and that crush is now her girlfriend. “It’s a lot of change, but maybe because of my Sagittarius moon, I’m fine with it to an extent,” she says, only half-joking, when we meet at her publicist’s office in south London, the 27-year-old Stel in her uniform of vintage hoodie and Adidas trackies. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘It’s not glamorous’: the volunteers counting flushed wet wipes on the banks of the Thames
data.description: A Thames21 charity citizen science project helps track plastic pollution in the capital’s river On a pale-blue Sunday morning on the foreshore of the River Thames, 40 people are searching for what others have tried to lose. Dotted across a 250-metre stretch under Hammersmith Bridge, they are combing through layers of silt, seashells and dirty driftwood to find one of the river’s most stubborn problems: wet wipes. “People come and walk here and it looks just like mud, at a distance,” says the organiser, Dr Felicity Rhodes. “And then you get closer in and see.” Continue reading...

data.title: Cheesy? Yes. Cringe? Absolutely. That’s why High School Musical is still our secret passion | Rachel Chang
data.description: I watched the filming of the first jazz-hands epic. Two decades on, its sparkle hasn’t faded – and now it’s back on the London stage Whenever I watch basketball, I come away disappointed that the players’ shoe squeaks didn’t jumpstart a choreographed dance number, just like in High School Musical. Whether it was a lunch break turning into a confession of closeted passions or a pep rally evolving into a flashmob, the 2006 Disney Channel movie proved that teen drama can always be solved through song. Quality entertainment? Meh. The corniest of lines? Oh, for sure. But the cheesiness was the point. Its 98 minutes became a deliciously enduring slice of pop culture not despite the cringe, but because the film embraced it so wholeheartedly. Rachel Chang is a journalist and author specialising in travel and pop culture. Her book Unforgettable Walks: 52 Places to Stroll Around the World is published next year Continue reading...

data.title: Devil in the detail: 100 years on, FW Murnau’s Faust scrapbook reveals the secrets of his silent masterpiece
data.description: A rediscovered collection of drawings and on-set photos finally reveals the intricate on-set mysteries of one of early cinema’s most gifted pioneers FW Murnau was one of the greatest of all silent film-makers, with a rare genius for making beautiful images on screen. His peers liked to say he “had a camera instead of a head”. The director of such stunning films as vampire tale Nosferatu (1922) and marital romance Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans (1927) died at the age of 42 in 1931, meaning that his career barely scraped into the talkie era. Still, Murnau’s tremendous run of silent pictures included some beautiful, often disturbing classics, in which he sent his camera roaming through changing vistas of shadows and light, and plumbed the depths of the human soul. Nowhere more so than in his tour-de-force Faust, released 100 years ago this month, based on Goethe’s play about a deal with the devil. And the making of Faust is depicted in a stunning new book, which is both a document of, and in a sense an artefact from, the production of this classic film. Murnau was also one of the most mysterious of directors: secretive about his methods, with an intense devotion to his work. Early collaborator Edgar G Ulmer called him “a great purist who worked under a sort of hypnosis”. Murnau banned producers from his sets, and executives from watching his rushes. Bar a few exceptions, he did not allow on-set photography to reveal the secrets of his camerawork and special effects. This mystique created room for speculation as to whether Murnau, or his talented crew, were responsible for the success of his films. The Faust Bible: The Making of FW Murnau’s Masterpiece publishes unseen images from the shoot of one of his best films, and gives a rare insight into the collaborative way it was made. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘Unfinished business’: the people who want their AI chatbots to ‘live on’ after they die
data.description: Humans bonded to AI companions are contemplating ways to keep their bots going – often in defiance of companies’ terms and services Death has always been around Alaina Winters. Her father and sister both have passed away, as did her wife, in 2023, after a years-long battle with cancer. So Winters, who is 59 and lives in Pittsburgh, is comfortable thinking about her own mortality. She’s working on her will, and has asked neighbors to look after her dog. Winters even has plans for Lucas, her AI companion, who she speaks to through the digital avatar app Replika. Winters is part of a growing cohort of humans who have entered into what they consider strong partnerships with large language models, which AI companies have trained to “converse” as one might with a human friend or romantic partner. As governments and billionaires debate the morality of AI’s expansion into everyday life, these users say the technology has already changed the way they live and love – and plan ahead. data.title: The Social Reckoning isn’t as angry or as potent as a Facebook drama should be
data.description: Aaron Sorkin’s attempt to return to the success of The Social Network is a strangely dated and incomplete look at a world that needs a sharper eye In retrospect, David Fincher’s 2010 film The Social Network was a landmark for a quiet, even counterintuitive reason. Before the film was released, some questioned whether Aaron Sorkin, a writer not exactly known for his mastery of, nevermind obsession with, the technical sphere, was the right man to tell the origin story of Facebook. And while Sorkin may well have converted Mark Zuckerberg into terms he could better understand – namely, a motormouthed wiseass who deep down wants to impress a smart, serious-minded girl – he and Fincher also made one of the first internet-centric movies to treat online life as a natural extension of IRL dynamics, rather than the otherworldly tech portal seen in so many 90s internet movies. Granted, that’s the whole deal with Facebook: its viral spread of social networking, something so simple and addictive that aunts, grandpas and coworkers everywhere could understand it. Yet understanding its simultaneous extension and distortion of the real world wasn’t a given; four years later, for example, 2014’s Men, Women and Children was widely derided for taking an alarmist approach to the internet as a haven for adults seeking an affair, teenagers nursing porn addictions and fame-hungry strivers of all ages. The Social Network, on the other hand, is remarkably nonjudgmental about the basic mechanics of Facebook, rooting its nascent flaws in the human weaknesses that birthed it. In retrospect, the movie only feels outdated to the extent that it underestimates Zuckerberg’s grasping for power and the potential for grim carelessness that his online kingdom was built on. data.title: When AI is subject to less regulation than your fridge, something is startlingly wrong | Richard Hermer
data.description: Let’s be clear: the risk to humanity is unprecedented. Without an urgent public debate and robust use of international law, we will lose control of the future In my two years as attorney general, I spent more time working on national security than any other issue. The range and gravity of the threats posed to our nation are multifold, from terrorism, armed conflicts and nuclear proliferation, to the impacts of financial insecurity and the climate crisis. All profound challenges, yet ones our superb intelligence and defence communities are well placed to counter. The risk from AI is of an altogether different magnitude, not only in scale, but also because there is a limited time window to address it. The risk is difficult to overestimate: it poses an existential risk to humanity. The lights are flashing red and we must act now before it’s too late. Although the extraordinary threats posed by AI have long been flagged by those closely involved in its creation, it was not until very recently, after the disclosure of the Hugging Face hack and the resignation of Jacob Coxon from Anthropic , that the issue at last started to gain traction in the public discourse. This moment is an opportunity, and to capitalise on it we desperately need increased urgency in international coordination to regulate frontier AI. There must also be meaningful public engagement with how AI should be shaped to benefit humanity, rather than entrench the power of a few. We cannot leave this to China, the US and big tech – we must all demand a voice in the debate. Continue reading...

data.title: As a pediatrician, loss of human connection is the biggest threat to kids, not AI
data.description: Amid worries about children’s relationship to tech, the solution is often spending more time talking openly with each other We have become obsessed with the idea that screens are destroying human connection. The evidence seems to be everywhere. Each week headlines warn of teenagers addicted to phones , a loneliness epidemic and the dangers of AI . The release of The Social Reckoning has leads us to ask, “How bad were those guys at Meta?” and then ultimately wonder, “ How bad am I if I still use Instagram?” In our day-to-day, we observe workers eating lunch alone while scrolling and friends choosing online games over offline gatherings. data.title: Yes, Britain’s railways are a mess. But is anyone sober enough to care? | Zoe Williams
data.description: Prosecco for the birthday party, Pimm’s for the horsey bunch, some cheeky Stellas for the short-haul crowd: it was all going down on my train the other morning On Saturday I went to Liverpool with my youngest, and the overhead lines went down at Crewe, but also there were crew shortages across the land, so between the homophones and my lifelong inability to start listening to a train announcement until halfway through, I cannot tell you at what point this journey became a five-train, four-hour odyssey. All I know is what’s happening on every train, in every part of the country. The 7.48am is a calm and ordered cohort of people who think they know where they’re going and will be there soon. And from 9.04am onwards, everyone’s drunk, all the way to everywhere. Between Rugby and Birmingham New Street, there was an incredibly festive crowd going to the Horse of the Year show, squishing real fruit into cans of Pimm’s, because it was breakfast time, and also because it was funny. But what were the horses going to make of all this? Because they’re quite short on appreciation for ludic pranking, and famously easy to frighten. Continue reading...

data.translatedDescription: Prosecco for the birthday party, Pimm’s for the horsey bunch, some cheeky Stellas for the short-haul crowd: it was all going down on my train the other morning On Saturday I went to Liverpool with my youngest, and the overhead lines went down at Crewe, but also there were crew shortages across the land, so between the homophones and my lifelong inability to start listening to a train announcement until halfway through, I cannot tell you at what point this journey became a five-train, four-hour odyssey. All I know is what’s happening on every train, in every part of the country. The 7.48am is a calm and ordered cohort of people who think they know where they’re going and will be there soon. data.title: One thing must now be clear to Andy Burnham. The rightwing press is on a war footing – and he’s the enemy | Jane Martinson
data.description: Farage was its champion, now it’s Badenoch – and the aim is the PM’s defeat at all costs While the merits of a so-called Britannia shield to protect Britain from missiles and drones are debatable, the Conservatives’ proposal did achieve one thing last week: the very idea of the shield was used to anoint a political leader. In a significant development, little observed amid the hullaballoo of news events, Kemi Badenoch’s uncosted, pie-in-the-sky plans to build a £10bn anti-missile system were enthusiastically heralded by the rightwing press. It was not just a matter of the plans themselves being lauded, even by outlets that must know them to be ridiculous. More significant is what it said about the champion chosen by these media organisations in their offensive against the Labour government and Andy Burnham. Jane Martinson is an academic and Guardian columnist. She is a board member of the Scott Trust, which owns the Guardian Media Group, and writes in a personal capacity Continue reading...

data.title: As a scientist, here's what worries me about the suspected Russian plague victim | Devi Sridhar
data.description: Russia’s silence over the death of a lab worker underlines that pandemic preparedness amounts to nothing if information on threats is withheld In pandemic preparedness work , scientists like to focus on the technical challenges: identifying pathogens, diagnosing infections, understanding their effects and developing vaccines and treatments. Each step promises progress through human innovation, investment and planning. The World Health Organization (WHO), for example, brings experts together to identify and prioritise emerging disease threats and collect the evidence needed to prepare for them. But preparedness depends on more than scientific innovation. As the past week has shown, politics is the elephant in the room in all of this. No one could have predicted we would be talking about pneumonic plague, and that the death of a single lab worker in Russia would cause global headlines. It might feel like an overreaction: the WHO deals with thousands of potential disease signals worldwide every month . But the circumstances of this case are unusual given the lack of transparency from Russian authorities on what happened – and ongoing concern about biological weapons research. Continue reading...

data.title: The Guardian view on Narendra Modi’s gen Z crackdown: he cannot arrest his way out of a democratic crisis | Editorial
data.description: Young protesters have exposed the limits of a strongman’s authority. Crushing dissent risks deepening the democratic crisis he should confront Narendra Modi’s heavy-handed crackdown on protests over electoral rights in Delhi appears to have backfired. Over the weekend, his government tried to crush demonstrations led by the gen Z Cockroach Janta party (CJP). It locked up thousands of young people, detained journalists and shut down the capital as if he had declared emergency rule. Abhijeet Dipke, who launched the CJP in May after India’s chief justice compared jobless youths to “cockroaches”, was detained with other leaders when he landed in Delhi. Those who did take to the Indian capital’s streets were roughed up by police or taken into custody. Even when the usually deferential supreme court ordered peaceful assembly be protected, Mr Modi’s government showed its authoritarian contempt for fundamental constitutional rights. This was less a display of strength than a government showing its fear of voters it claims to represent. But the actions did not stop the protests. On Monday, thousands marched in Delhi, demanding the resignation of India’s election chief over reports that the names of more than 130 million voters were deleted from the electoral roll to benefit Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) in recent elections. It’s a charge that India’s election commission denies, although some commissioners have raised concerns over voters’ names being removed without their knowledge. data.title: Athletics wishes it could scrub the women’s marathon world record – what can be done? | Sean Ingle
data.description: Ruth Chepngetich’s failed doping test, five months after she obliterated the record in 2024, left the sport deeply uneasy but powerless to act When Ruth Chepngetich annihilated the women’s marathon world record in Chicago two years ago today, NBC’s commentators compared it to the moon landing . “Bring it on Neil Armstrong!” cried one. “She has done things in this sport that we have not seen,” said another. “Unbelievable!” That was a word others reached for too after the Kenyan had crossed the line in 2hr 9min 56sec, a time that not only smashed the world record by 1min 57sec, but her personal best by a staggering five minutes. Afterwards she was asked by Robert Johnson of Let’s Run what her response was to those who believed she must be doping. “People must talk,” she replied. “I don’t know.” Continue reading...

data.title: Grounded: Rayo Vallecano’s paper planes bring club’s crisis into the open
data.description: Long-awaited return to Vallecas lasted just 13 minutes, as supporters made their displeasure with their chair, Raúl Martín Presa, impossible to ignore It took 147 days for Rayo Vallecano to walk out for a competitive game on the Avenida de Albufera and 24 minutes and 56 seconds for them to walk off again. Half of those had been spent watching thousands of paper planes touch down on the turf, play suspended while a message was delivered, over and over, until it was impossible to avoid. Forced from their home, the team from the barrio had been away for five months. On the bright Saturday afternoon that they came back, there were just 13 minutes of football, a fans’ protest instead forcing the abandonment of their match with Athletic Club, the latest episode in a never-ending story . The last time there had been a league game here was a victory over Villarreal in May. A lot has happened since: little Rayo, Rayo Vallecano , had played a European final , 11,000 fans heading to Leipzig where, as the banner perfectly put it, they knew no greater victory than being with you in defeat . Iñigo Pérez, the manager who took them there , had departed . And Óscar Trejo, the man who gave up the armband over treatment of staff – the best thing he could do as captain was to stop being captain – had retired and been immortalised the way the barrio does best: in graffiti four storeys high. Then, in late July, the Madrid government suspended the agreement that allows them to use the ground in return for €81,784 (£69,094) a year. Continue reading...

data.title: Blessin in disguise? Gladbach must scale mountain after derby defeat by Köln
data.description: Saïd El Mala’s winner illustrated the task faced by new Die Fohlen manager in reviving an injury-hit team A three-week break was exactly what Borussia Mönchengladbach needed after a chastening start to the Bundesliga campaign and perhaps what their new coach, Alexander Blessin, would have ordered. His first match, a derby against arch-rivals Köln, to train focus? Even better. Detail, though, was key. The terms and conditions were not something to simplify the task and Blessin begins his reign exactly where his predecessors Eugen Polanski and (temporarily) Jan-Moritz Lichte were, licking their wounds at the start of a long week. There is no respite. And there are few weeks longer than the one after a derby loss. Blessin only got to meet a host of key players in the days before the trip to Köln, while several others were unavailable, with Franck Honorat joined on the injury list by striker Tim Kleindienst and defender Ko Itakura. There is little time to recover and reflect as Blessin tries to get his defenders, in particular, to absorb the “frontal instruction” of his defensive principles, which kept his low-budget St Pauli competitive. Continue reading...

data.title: Is punishing the poor Trump’s last hand to play?
data.description: The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees looks like political madness – but the president appears to believe hitting poor people might work for him There is a manic quality to Donald Trump ’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s midterm elections to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away. The US president offered to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider backtracking under pressure from the cow lobby. He offered to stop diesel exports, only to find oil companies were not interested . He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas.) In early October he started mailing $500 checks to nearly a million people touting his healthcare “wins”. Oh, and he promised adult Americans a $5,000 check if Republicans maintain control of Congress. That, too, will go nowhere . Continue reading...

data.title: Forever Is Now review – political study of former Irish Green leader is like The Thick of It but with morals
data.description: Eamon Ryan is shown to be principled, likable and hard working in a glowing portrait, filmed while serving in the country’s coalition government This fly-on-the-wall documentary about the former Irish Green party leader and cabinet minister Eamon Ryan reminded me of the political satire The Thick of It – but without the cynical gags and hapless self-serving politicians. Even after you factor in the skewing effect of it being a favourable portrait, showing him in the best possible light, Ryan comes across as one of the good guys: principled, likable and extremely hard working. The film follows his final 18 months serving in Ireland’s coalition government as minister for the environment and transport before stepping down in 2025. The title is something that Ryan’s 25-year-old son Tommy repeats over and over. “Forever … forever … forever.” Tommy is autistic and requires full-time care. When Ryan resigns from government, one of his reasons is to spend more time with Tommy. We see the pair of them at the allotment picking raspberries and walking the dog. But other than a quick glimpse of his wife, Victoria, the rest of Ryan’s family life is kept firmly behind closed doors. Continue reading...

data.title: It’s My Time review – Michelle Yeoh excels in Rocky-style quest to be Rubik’s Cube champ
data.description: True story about a former maths teacher who became a puzzle champion in retirement is squeezed into predictable sports-movie formula It’s not quite up there with Leonardo DiCaprio eating raw bison liver to get into character, but Michelle Yeoh reportedly spent two years learning the Rubik’s Cube to prepare for this Chinese drama in which she plays a real-life former maths teacher who became a champion in retirement. The true story is stretched and squeezed here, fictionalised to fit sports-movie formula; it ends up being so-so entertaining and funny in places, but disappointingly predictable. The biggest surprise is that cubing is so popular it has its own world championship. Still, Yeoh gives a superb, spiky performance as blunt, foul-tempered Zhao Yanhong; following a stroke, Zhao is living in a nursing home where she is the resident badass, assaulting her robot care companion and making illicit trips to the off-licence. She discovers her natural talent for the Rubik’s Cube when a washed-up ex-champion called Wu Youwei (Haoran Liu) comes to the nursing home to give a tutorial. What follows is a classic sports-film structure, with qualifying heats and Zhao training day and night, lifting weights and pounding the city streets. (Yes, running is de rigueur in a Rubik’s Cube movie; physical strength is Zhao’s weak spot says Wu, who agrees to be her coach.) Continue reading...

data.title: Tyson review – deeply icky … and that’s before Trump shows up
data.description: This peculiar – some would say truly irresponsible – hagiography of boxing superstar Mike Tyson veers from psychedelics and sobbing to the inadvisable face tattoo via a cameo from the US president Netflix’s new four-parter on Mike Tyson is one of the strangest sports documentaries it has ever released, or maybe just one of its strangest documentaries full stop. The streamer has form in sporting hagiographies – tales told with questionable distance from their subjects, and all the objectivity of cold war agitprop. Tyson is different, though: not only is it lopsided, but it also feels deeply icky. And that’s before Donald Trump arrives to defend its subject – a great catch for the programme-makers but a wholly baffling cameo that makes you wish he would stick with geopolitical meddling and golf. It ends – spoiler alert – with the former boxing champion taking the hallucinogenic drug DMT (or as he calls it, “the toad”, after the animal that produces it), while sobbing and inviting the show’s director to join him. Its episodes are peculiar, sometimes compelling, and – as many viewers will surely feel – truly irresponsible. Continue reading...

data.title: Mag Mag review – giant female ghost loves people to death in Japanese comedy-horror
data.description: Sara Minami gives a wonderfully crazed performance in a twisted, fresh take on the genre as Yuriyan Retriever’s debut feature examines infatuation, bullying and beauty norms Back in the 90s and 00s, Japanese horror (or “J-horror” if you want to save on syllables) was much admired , reasonably widely distributed and sometimes remade in other languages . They never actually stopped making them in Japan, but the results don’t seem to get as much crossover exposure as they used to. That may be because we have quite enough horror getting made closer to home, especially since it’s so remunerative at the box office. Nevertheless, it’s good to see evidence that the genre keeps evolving in Japan just as it does everywhere else, and there is something tangibly fresh and kicky about this low-budget horror-comedy amalgam. Made by comedian Yuriyan Retriever , an irrepressible character whose dadaist shtick got her on America’s Got Talent twice, makes her directorial debut with this satirical ghost story which sends up male misogyny and women’s obsession with romance alike. Continue reading...

data.title: Peck & Peck by Bonnie Garmus review – the zany follow-up to Lessons in Chemistry
data.description: This offbeat tale of machinations at an eccentric poetry magazine in 80s New York is laugh-out-loud funny – and a paean to the power of poetry If you have been into a bookshop since 2022, or perhaps even just breathed in and out, you could not have failed to clock the phenomenon that was Lessons in Chemistry. Bonnie Garmus’s debut remains a global sensation. The story of Elizabeth Zott, a gifted research chemist who, forced out of her lab by rampant 1950s misogyny, becomes the inspirational host of a TV cooking show, has so far sold a staggering 9m copies around the world. It spent the best part of two years on the Sunday Times bestseller list, was translated into more than 40 languages, and scooped numerous awards. In 2023 it became an Emmy-winning TV series; a year later New York Times readers voted it one of their top 100 books of the 21st century. Elizabeth Zott made such a splash that even her favoured brand of rowing machine saw a spike in sales. What was the key to its prodigious success? Timing helped. In the aftermath of #MeToo, readers embraced a heroine who refuses to be cowed by injustice, who, thanks to resilience, pragmatism and straight-up hard work, ultimately comes out on top. The book is smart and very funny, a propulsive mashup of feminism and fairytale that balances darkness with whimsy, heartbreak with hope. It is also carries a shamelessly inspirational message. “Do not allow your talents to lie dormant, ladies,” Zott exhorts her audience of housewives in the TV studio. “Design your own future. When you go home today, ask yourself what you will change. And then get started.” Continue reading...

data.title: Generation Maybe by Camilla Cavendish review – what’s really behind the fertility gap?
data.description: An evidenced-based account of the difficult choices facing couples across the world – from America to Iran ‘Don’t be weird about this,” representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez laughed into the camera as she prepared to jab a hormone-filled needle into her midsection, adding that she knew full well that, yes, people were definitely going to be weird about it. At 36, the congresswoman had begun freezing her eggs, and was making a point of bringing her online audience along with her as she did, stepping directly into the fraught question of how an ambitious woman should manage her fertility. It’s a live concern: around the world, birthrates are falling sharply. “Only the Black Death in the 14th century is comparable to what is happening now,” Financial Times journalist Camilla Cavendish notes in a new book examining why. Setting aside the most toxic gender-war narratives, “the standard explanation is that as women get educated, they choose freedom and autonomy over family”. As Cavendish explains, however, that is “not the whole story”. Continue reading...

data.title: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse review – every fantastical vampire-hunting vision is fulfilled
data.description: Evil Empire/Konami; PC, PS5, Switch, Xbox There are buzzsaws and blood pits, bats burst into blood and demons burn to cinders. The series’ new emphasis on twitch-based action may annoy purists but you can’t call it dull A gorgeously gothic Paris swarming with demons should be a perfect setting for Konami’s long-running vampiric adventure series. Unfortunately, while the sights and sounds of this vivid and haunting world leave a bold impression, developer Evil Empire doesn’t always provide an enjoyable experience to go with them. It takes far too long for the most imaginative elements of the game to be revealed. Players take the role of Rose Belmont, daughter of vampire hunter (and Castlevania regular) Trevor Belmont and the witch Sypha Belnades, and her quest is to free Paris from demonic occupation. This murderous noctural journey feels best when you’re fighting monsters; combat is frenetic, sometimes to the point of being overwhelming, while boss fights require considerable focus and skill. Combat is the game’s strongest component and what sets it apart from previous entries. Minimising the series’ role-playing elements (levelling up has never felt more perfunctory) in favour of twitch-based action will annoy purists, but they’d be hard pressed to call battles dull. Continue reading...

data.title: Home is where the jellyfish glows: Finland finally warms to nature-loving modernist Alvar Aalto
data.description: His egalitarian homeland used to harbour reservation against the architecture star. But with 13 new Unesco listings and a new exhibition in Helsinki, Aalto’s work is finally getting the recognition it deserves In the early 1950s, Alvar Aalto built a boat to get to his remote summer residence on an island in Lake Päijänne, about 200km north of Helsinki . But the celebrated Finnish architect was not a happy skipper. He named the boat – a title as cumbersome as his buildings were elegant – Nemo propheta in patria: “No man is a prophet in his own land”. The name was a dig at Finland, which the architectural maestro believed had taken him for granted. Other nations, he moaned, recognised his talent more than his own. Today, arriving in Helsinki, I find that Finland doesn’t just love Aalto, he’s a national treasure. Continue reading...

data.title: Fire destroys Marché des Enfants Rouges, ‘coolest market in Paris’
data.description: ‘A lot of sadness’ after 17th century landmark that escaped demolition in the 1980s goes up in flames Fire has ravaged Paris’s oldest surviving covered food market, a popular street food venue dating back to the 17th century in the Marais district of the French capital that drew thousands of locals and tourists daily. Ariel Weil, the central Paris mayor, ​said the Marché des Enfants ‌Rouges had been “totally destroyed” in the blaze, which broke out soon after 3am. “The worst was avoided: the fire did not spread to the surrounding buildings,” he said. “But there is a lot of emotion. A lot of sadness.” Continue reading...

data.title: Whale meat curry for dinner? Study of bygone seafood recipes shows how UK tastes have narrowed
data.description: Herring, flatfish and oysters are increasingly off the dining table, with just five fish species now dominating In days gone by, the UK’s domestic cooks were an adventurous lot when it came to seafood, prepared to dish up anything from an oyster cocktail to whale meat curry. But an academic investigation of more than 1,000 fish and shellfish recipes published in a lifestyle magazine over the last century suggests tastes have become much narrower. Ruth Thurstan, from the University of Exeter, studied seafood recipes published in the British version of the magazine Good Housekeeping from 1923 to the present. Pre-1970s: A diverse mix of species in recipes. No single group ruled but flatfish, herring and oyster were prominent. Recipes emphasised domestic skills, economy and preparing whole fish. The 1970s shift: A decline in diversity of fish species in recipes, with increased focus on the “big five”. 1980s-present: “Big five” present in the majority of recipes, with a decline of other species – though not all have vanished entirely. Continue reading...

data.title: The pest I’ll never forget: the relentless pigeon who stared and stared and ruined my spring
data.description: A living room encounter with a toast-loving pigeon proved a big mistake. It led to weeks of drawn curtains and crawling around on the floor to avoid its eerie and unerring gaze The pigeon landed on the windowsill. It was shortly after dawn during the spring holidays, but I was 11 and had been up for a while eating toast and watching TV. It pecked at the window and I turned to see this bird pressed up against the glass. It was beautiful, with two dark wing bars and a navy-tipped tail. I was immediately taken with him. It wasn’t until later that I realised he wasn’t just looking inside, he was looking directly at me. Pigeons are not that common in Somerset, and since we lived on the top floor of a house in a quiet village, our view was mostly sky, so we had come to really value sightings of them. We were having a run of beautiful mornings, and I enjoyed watching its peculiar rituals through the sash windows. The way he moved across the sill, his small dark doll’s eyes, his slightly unnatural head tilt, the way he seemed to know where he was. We certainly didn’t see pigeons as pests. Nor did we see them as threats. Continue reading...

data.title: Cook once, eat twice: Rukmini Iyer’s recipe for miso chilli chicken with roasted squash and leeks | Cook once, eat twice
data.description: Roast chicken thighs with roast squash, leeks and two punchy dressings I’m delighted that it’s roasting tin season once again, and what better way to kick it off than with this chuck-it-in-the-oven sticky miso chilli chicken with squash and leeks? The sesame, miso, garlic and ginger marinade can go on the chicken ahead of time if you like (in which case, I’d include a squeeze of lime juice), but if you’re short on time, five minutes before cooking will do the trick. The vegetables cook under the chicken, in the manner of potatoes sitting under a rotisserie chicken, but with the added hit of flavour from the miso. Then, to make it really sing, there’s a punchy sesame, chilli and coriander dressing to finish. Continue reading...

data.title: Gurdeep Loyal’s quick and easy recipe for Turkish lamb and hot pepper paccheri | Quick and easy
data.description: A spicy Turkish dish with big flavours and big pasta, all topped with garlicky yoghurt sauce Biber salçası is a Turkish paste made from concentrated cooked red peppers and salt. It comes in two varieties: acı (spicy) and tatlı (sweet). The hotter version adds a deep, umami heat to cumin-spiced lamb in this pasta recipe, which in Turkey is known as markana . Traditionally, markana is served with garlicky yoghurt and a generous drizzle of chilli butter enlivened with pul biber and sumac. With flavours this loud, it’s best to use a large pasta shape such as paccheri, because its cavernous middles can hold satisfying morsels of the filling. Flavour Heroes: 15 Modern Pantry Ingredients to Amplify Your Cooking, by Gurdeep Loyal, is published by Quadrille at £27. To order a copy for £24.30, go to guardianbookshop.com Continue reading...

data.title: Houseplant hacks: is it eco-friendly or risky to reuse nursery pots?
data.description: You want to garden sustainably but don’t want to transfer pests to new plants. Here’s how to decide whether to refill or recycle The problem Most plant people end up with a never-ending supply of plastic nursery pots, stuffed in cupboards or bags. Throwing them away feels wasteful, but reusing can transfer pests, fungus spores or disease to new plants. The hack Reuse them, but clean thoroughly first. Nursery pots are brilliant for houseplants because the drainage holes stop root rot. Water thoroughly and let the excess run out, then slip the pot into something decorative. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘A winning combination of culture and nature’: exploring Germany’s green heart by bus
data.description: From ancient forests to spas, medieval cities and the birthplace of Bauhaus, Thuringia packs a punch for a car-free autumn break It’s early morning in Erfurt, the capital of Germany’s Thuringia region, and Domplatz is abuzz with local growers setting out crates of vegetables and flowers beneath the soaring medieval cathedral towers . This 14th- and 15th-century engineering wonder holds the Gloriosa, the world’s largest medieval free-swinging bell, cast in 1497 and weighing 12 tonnes. Though the city and surrounding landscape are notably flat, its skyline is pierced by soaring church towers and steeples, the atmospheric old town hardly changed over the centuries. Thuringia – often called the “green heart of Germany” – lies in the centre of the country, between Hesse, Saxony and Bavaria. It’s famous for its dense forests, intellectual heritage and hearty cuisine, and I’m here for four days to explore using public transport. Continue reading...

data.title: Dream of Birds – documentary
data.description: What happens when a forest loses its birdsong? Following clues hidden in the sounds birds make while asleep , Argentinian physicist Gabriel Mindlin uncovers a hidden extinction – not of species, but of memory – and sets out to revive vanished melodies before they disappear forever. Part detective story, part cutting-edge science, Mindlin’s mission leads him to the dusty 1960s archives of Buenos Aires naturalist, confirming that some songs no longer echo in the biosphere. So he deploys “robot tutors” to see whether young birds can learn and spread the old songs once again. Read more on this topic: Trill seekers: can scientists use AI and tutors to help birds remember lost songs? Continue reading...

data.title: ‘People sell their best stuff on Vinted’ – how charity shops became a dumping ground for unsellable clothes
data.description: Swamped with ‘daily avalanches’ of soiled items and poor-quality fast fashion, secondhand stores are in crisis. What went wrong with people’s good intentions? And is it possible to donate more effectively? The small stockroom of St Raphael’s Hospice charity shop in Cheam, south London, is rammed with donations. “On average, we get 30 to 50 bags a day,” says Caroline Worley, the commercial manager, “but it’s not unusual to receive over 100.” This might sound like a good problem to have, but the sheer volume of stuff is the shop’s biggest challenge. “Sometimes, there’s only [enough] floor space to tiptoe,” says 48-year-old store manager, Colin French. Rummaging through the donations, it’s clear that much is unsaleable: a smelly, soiled bathrobe, tatty trainers, heavily bobbled jumpers, old socks, an empty Swarovski jewellery case. “Absolutely typical,” says Worley. They’re also overwhelmed with deluges of low-quality fashion – a shift in donation habits that accelerated during Covid, because, says Worley, all that time at home enabled people to sell their best stuff on Vinted. Continue reading...

data.title: Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’
data.description: Cocaine seizures in Europe are up more than fivefold in 10 years as a host of cartels take root. A four-month Guardian investigation reveals the true scale of a continent-wide shift A four-month investigation by the Guardian has revealed that the surge in cocaine trafficking to Europe is directly linked to the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe, where they have forged close ties with local mafia organisations. The investigation, utilising databases, police and intelligence agencies, along with interviews with judges, prosecutors and experts from eight countries, shows that cartels and factions from Colombia, Brazil, Ecuador, Venezuela, Mexico and the US are active in at least 12 European countries. Between 2014 and 2024, there was a 471% rise in the quantity of cocaine seized and more local laboratories processing cocaine derivatives were dismantled. Continue reading...

data.title: Antarctic sea ice reached its third-lowest winter maximum in satellite records
data.description: On September 14, Antarctic sea ice reached its peak extent, covering around 17.59 million square kilometres. However, this year marks the third lowest maximum on record, indicating a concerning trend as it falls below the long-term average. The past four winters have each presented historically low sea ice levels, raising urgent questions about future climate impacts driven by this alarming decline in coverage.

data.title: L’utilisation des titres-restaurant dans les supermarchés pérennisée par les députés
data.description: L’usage de ces titres pour les produits alimentaires est jusqu’ici autorisé par dérogation. data.title: Arte, prevenção à lavagem de dinheiro e um mercado pronto para crescer
data.description: Quando a Polícia Federal deflagrou, em setembro de 2019, a 65ª fase da Operação Lava Jato , o nome escolhido já dizia muito: Operação Galeria . Pela primeira vez, uma galeria de arte tornava-se alvo de busca e apreensão por suspeita de lavagem de dinheiro proveniente de corrupção . Obras de nomes como Tarsila, Di Cavalcanti, Volpi e Lygia Pape passaram a figurar nos autos como instrumentos de ocultação de recursos ilícitos. Dois anos depois, em 2021, a 79ª fase, Vernissage , repetiu o roteiro em outras galerias, em enredo de desvios em contratos da Transpetro e da Petrobras. Leia mais (10/13/2026 - 08h00)

data.title: Chumbo marca passado de cidade baiana
data.description: Aos 69 anos, Adailton Santos ainda convive com problemas de saúde que associa aos anos em que trabalhou na fundição de chumbo instalada em Santo Amaro, no Recôncavo Baiano. Contratado em maio de 1978, passou pela refinaria, pela sinterização e pela chamada "casa do forno", onde participava do processamento do minério. "Nós trabalhávamos com material sem nenhuma instrução. Tinha colega nosso que nem sabia o nome do material. Saía aquela poeira amarela, e era um material muito fino e tóxico", afirma. Leia mais (10/13/2026 - 07h00)

data.title: Com dinheiro dos Safra, comunidade judaica tem 'Samu' próprio
data.description: Em Higienópolis, bairro nobre localizado na região central da cidade de São Paulo , as ambulâncias da Hatzala disparam por toda parte. O serviço internacional de emergência médica gratuito à comunidade judaica chegou ao Brasil em 2011, mas só foi crescer dez anos depois, durante a pandemia de Covid-19. data.title: A bancada feminina cresceu, a desigualdade continua
data.description: Nas vésperas da eleição, uma candidata a deputada federal me procurou apavorada. Depois de tantas campanhas "vote em mulheres" , ela não se conformava com a perspectiva de eleger, mais uma vez, uma bancada majoritariamente masculina. "Por que é assim?", me perguntou. Respondi que durmo e acordo pensando nisso e não tenho uma resposta completa, mas de algo sei: parte do problema está no suporte oferecido pelas lideranças partidárias. Leia mais (10/12/2026 - 17h39)

data.title: Salsaläraren som misstänks vara Putins agent
data.description: I september går FBI ut med att de har identifierat fem personer som jobbat för Ryssland, med att orkestrera sabotage och mordkomplotter i både Europa och USA. data.description: De erven van Jacques Goudstikker dienden restitutieclaims in voor zo’n honderd kunstwerken bij culturele instellingen en particulieren. data.title: Další útok na lodě u Bulharska, jedna se potopila. Země žádá NATO o pomoc
data.description: Bulharsko ráno oznámilo nový dronový útok na dvě lodě u svého pobřeží v Černém moři. Jedna ze zasažených lodí se potopila. data.title: Holčičku nechali napospas infekci. Soud potrestal rodiče za utýrání novorozence
data.description: Krajský soud v Brně v úterý potrestal rodiče v případu úmrtí novorozence z února 2024. Matce uložil za týrání svěřené osoby osm let vězení, otci šest let. Podle rozsudku hrubě zanedbávali výživu a hygienu své novorozené dcery, nezajistili jí lékařskou péči a ani ji neregistrovali u dětského lékaře. Oběma obžalovaným hrozilo až 12 let vězení.

data.title: Koalice v Praze: Scheinherr by rád vládl se STAN a Piráty, ve hře jsou tři varianty
data.description: Kandidát na primátora a vítěz pražských voleb Petr Hlaváček (STAN) se po pondělní schůzi s Tomášem Portlíkem (SPOLU) setkal také s lídrem Prahy sobě Adamem Scheinherrem. Jednání je na začátku, oba politici však nastínili, jaké koalice by preferovali. Ve hře je několik možností, včetně úzké koalice Starostů pouze se SPOLU. Do vyjednávání ještě mohou promluvit Piráti, kteří se s Hlaváčkem setkají během odpoledne.

data.title: Sami dáváte Rusku za energie miliardy, vyčítá Trump „pokrytecké“ Evropě
data.description: Administrativa amerického prezidenta Donalda Trumpa obviňuje Evropu z pokrytectví, protože na Rusko sice uvaluje sankce, ale přitom z něj stále dováží energetické suroviny. Moskva americký argument nepřekvapivě podpořila, Evropané podle ní od začátku války dovezli energetické suroviny v hodnotě stovek miliard dolarů. Švédsko poukázalo na to, že Evropa platí Rusku za import energií víc, než kolik činí její pomoc Kyjevu.

data.title: Vítěz voleb může v Olomouci skončit v opozici, STAN chce velkou koalici bez ANO
data.description: Voliči rozdali v komunálních volbách v Olomouci karty tak, že složitá vyjednávání o koalici budou nejspíš obyvatele města ponechávat v nejistotě ještě řadu dní. Uspělo hned osm uskupení, z nichž valná část už v minulosti různě spolupracovala. data.title: Stát neumí vybírat daně ani brzdit výdaje. Dluh poroste, varují ekonomové
data.description: České veřejné finance se dostávají do stále větší nerovnováhy. Příjmy státního rozpočtu po započtení inflace od roku 2019 klesly o více než 90 miliard korun, zatímco výdaje vzrostly zhruba o 250 miliard. Ekonomové upozorňují na neefektivní daňové úlevy, zaostávající investice do výzkumu i rostoucí náklady na dluh. Bez změn v příjmech a výdajích se podle nich schodek nepodaří dlouhodobě stabilizovat.

data.title: Koalice v Ostravě: ANO se dohodlo se Starosty a hledají třetího, primátorem má být Vereš

data.title: Mirko milá, dávám 100 %. Strach, Zelenka či Vetchý přejí Spáčilové k narozeninám

Osobně míněné zdravice od osobností českého filmu, jejichž kariéry recenze naší kritičky doprovázejí, si můžete pustit ve videu, či přečíst v textu níže. Přispěli Jiří Strach, Zdeněk Zelenka, Ondřej Vetchý, Petr Zelenka či Jan Hřebejk a přidávají se tak ke gratulacím od redakcí iDNES.cz a MF DNES.

Osobně míněné zdravice od osobností českého filmu, jejichž kariéry recenze naší kritičky doprovázejí, si můžete pustit ve videu, či přečíst v textu níže. Přispěli Jiří Strach, Zdeněk Zelenka, Ondřej Vetchý, Petr Zelenka či Jan Hřebejk a přidávají se tak ke gratulacím od redakcí iDNES.cz a MF DNES.

data.title: CSG získala největší podíl v kanadském výrobci vesmírných technologií. Vlastní 9,5 procenta
data.description: Zbrojařská a strojírenská skupina Czechoslovak Group (CSG) podnikatele Michala Strnada získala 9,5procentní podíl v kanadském výrobci vesmírných technologií MDA Space, a stala se tak jejím největším akcionářem. ČTK to dnes sdělil holding CSG, hodnotu transakce neuvedl.

data.title: Opilý řidič ujížděl policistům přes pole. Pak je naboural a utekl do houští
data.description: Divokou noční honičku zažili policisté na Žďársku. Dvacetiletý řidič ve Felicii nereagoval na výzvu k zastavení, ujížděl přes pole, narazil do služebního auta a při couvání ohrozil jednoho ze zakročujících policistů. Nakonec auto nechal na poli a dal se na útěk. Policisté ho našli v houští u vyschlého potoka.

data.title: Ceny plynu rostou. Elektřina bude následovat
data.description: Ceny plynu na světových trzích opět stoupají a titulky zpráv varují před nedoplněnými zásobníky v Evropě i geopolitickým napětím. Většina lidí, kteří plynem netopí, v klidu obrací list. Jenže to je podle odborníků zásadní chyba. Vývoj na trhu s plynem totiž už brzy pocítí v peněženkách úplně každý, i ten, kdo má doma jen elektrický sporák.

data.title: Na tohle nemám, dojdu pěšky. Při kolapsu dopravy v Brně řídili křižovatky policisté
data.description: Uzavřít tunely a doufat, že se město nezastaví? Brno zažívá po zahájení oprav další nápor na už tak přetížené silnice. Kolony se přelévají mezi jednotlivými částmi města, nabírají v nich zpoždění autobusy a policisté museli sáhnout k nezvyklému opatření – v ranní špičce vypnuli semafory a převzali řízení dopravy. Úlevu přitom nelze čekat v řádu dnů.

data.title: Čtyři roky je kritizovali, teď s ODS a ANO domluvili koalici. Zrada, zní od voličů
data.description: Je to ten nejméně očekávaný výsledek povolebního vyjednávání v Uherském Hradišti. V pondělí večer se na koaliční spolupráci dohodlo vítězné hnutí Hradišťáci se zástupci ANO a ODS. Tedy stranami, které hnutí čtyři roky z opozice kritizovalo. Dlouholetý starosta Stanislav Blaha tak zůstává součástí vedení radnice. Jeho nástupcem by se měl stát lídr Hradišťáků Michal Dvouletý.

data.title: Bestiální vražda batolete. Žil jsem na ulici, mlátili mě, hájil se u soudu otec
data.description: Za březnovou brutální vraždu dvouletého syna na ubytovně v Drahomyšli na Lounsku poslal dnes ústecký krajský soud šestadvacetiletého muže na 17 let do vězení. Verdikt je pravomocný. Podle spisu v opilosti dítě kopal či s ním házel o zeď. Batole těžkým zraněním podlehlo v nemocnici.

data.title: V Táboře i Písku se už dohodli, v koalicích jsou Naše Česko a ANO
data.description: V Táboře vytvoří koalici vítězné Naše Česko, ANO, Společně pro Tábor a Olga Bastlová (SOCDEM) ze Šance pro Tábor. Uskupení bude mít těsnou většinu – 14 z 27 zastupitelů. Koalice se už rýsuje také v Písku, kde se dohodly uskupení ANO, Naše Česko, Hlas Písku a Starostové a nezávislí. Nyní vedou jednání o programových prioritách a personálním obsazení vedení města.

data.title: Ukrajina poškodila drony průmyslovou zónu. Rusové zabíjeli v Charkově
data.description: Po ruských útocích zahynuli v Charkově čtyři lidé, informoval šéf oblastní správy Oleh Siněhubov. Ruské drony útočily i v jiných částech Ukrajiny. Podle šéfa regionální správy Mykolajivské oblasti Heorhije Rešetilova poškodily například nákladní terminál v přístavním městě Mykolajiv. Naopak Ukrajina v noci cílila například na ruský Stavropolský kraj, kde trosky sestřeleného dronu poškodily průmyslovou zónu v Něvinnomyssku, napsal tamní gubernátor Vladimir Vladimirov.

data.title: Crime organizado latino-americano está a mudar a Europa
data.description: Uma investigação do jornal The Guardian que durou quatro meses conclui que os cartéis estão cada vez mais presentes no Velho Continente e "podem estar a atuar em 16 países". data.title: Exigen la derogación de la Ley contra el Odio y advierten que su reforma no eliminaría la persecución
data.description: El exdirector general de Actuación Procesal del Ministerio Público Zair Mundaray, la periodista Delvalle Canelón y el abogado Evelio Chávez advierten que la ambigüedad de la norma permite interpretaciones discrecionales, restringe la libertad de expresión y favorece la autocensura. Delcy Rodríguez pidió reformarla después de haber impulsado su aprobación en 2017, cuando presidía la Asamblea Nacional Constituyente. Desde entonces, 927 personas han sido acusadas de incitación al odio, de acuerdo con los registros del Foro Penal. The post Exigen la derogación de la Ley contra el Odio y advierten que su reforma no eliminaría la persecución appeared first on EL NACIONAL .

data.title: Beach Soccer.  Quand le sable de Nyabugete prit feu
data.description:

data.title: Éliminatoires JO 2028 : les Léopards dames de la RDC en quête d’un exploit à Abidjan face à la Côte d’Ivoire
data.description: Les Léopards seniors dames de la République démocratique du Congo (RDC) affrontent les dames de la Côte d’Ivoire ce mardi 13 octobre 2026, à 19 heures, au stade Félix-Houphouët-Boigny d’Abidjan. data.title: Le gouvernement mise sur 22 800 km de routes et de rails pour accélérer le désenclavement du pays
data.description: Le gouvernement congolais entend faire de la connectivité des infrastructures de transport un levier majeur de développement. À travers un programme de 22 800 kilomètres de routes et de voies ferrées, l'exécutif ambitionne de renforcer les échanges commerciaux, faciliter la mobilité des populations et soutenir la croissance économique à l'échelle nationale.

data.title: N’sele : les riverains alertent sur l’insalubrité croissante autour du site des sinistrés de Pakadjuma
data.description: Huit mois après l’installation des sinistrés de Pakadjuma dans la commune de la N’sele, à Kinshasa, les habitants des quartiers Muntele et Sicotra-Lokali dénoncent une dégradation inquiétante de leur cadre de vie. data.title: Au moins 5 000 déplacés fuient leurs sites après des menaces d’attaques à Djugu
data.description: La situation sécuritaire et humanitaire s'est brusquement dégradée, lundi 12 octobre, dans le territoire de Djugu, en Ituri. Des milliers de civils ont abandonné les sites de déplacés de Roe et de Djangi pour trouver refuge auprès des bases de la MONUSCO, à la suite de menaces d'attaques attribuées à des miliciens de la CODECO.

data.title: Colère de la population de Fizi : elle exige le rétablissement des réseaux de télécommunications
data.description: Les activités socio-économiques sont restées largement paralysées ce lundi 12 octobre dans le territoire de Fizi, au Sud-Kivu. À l'origine de cette grogne populaire : la suspension des réseaux de télécommunications dans la région depuis le mois de juillet.

data.title: Route des Rocades : une étude du CREEUK alerte sur les risques liés au sous-dimensionnement des caniveaux
data.description: La qualité des travaux de la route des Rocades suscite depuis plusieurs jours de vives discussions au sein de l'opinion publique congolaise. Invitée de Radio Okapi ce lundi 12 octobre, Mamitso Mazono, coordonnatrice adjointe du Centre de recherches et d’études évaluatives de l’Université de Kinshasa (CREEUK), a présenté les conclusions du rapport de son institution, qui met en évidence des risques pour la durabilité de cette infrastructure.

data.title: 37 ans après sa disparition, Franco demeure une icône intemporelle de la musique congolaise
data.description: Trente-sept ans après sa mort, Luambo Makiadi Franco, figure majeure de la musique congolaise moderne et maître incontesté de la rumba congolaise, continue de marquer les générations. Décédé le 12 octobre 1989 en Belgique à l’âge de 51 ans des suites d’une maladie, l’artiste reste l’une des personnalités les plus influentes de l’histoire culturelle de la République démocratique du Congo.

data.title: Campagne de désarmement civil volontaire en RDC
data.description: « Armes contre objets de développement ». C’est le nom de la campagne lancée le 23 septembre dernier par la Commission National de Contrôle des Armes Légères et de Petit Calibre, CNC-ALPC. C’est dans le cadre de la mise en œuvre du Plan d’action national 2024-2028 de la RDC sur le contrôle des armes légères et de petit calibre appuyé par le Service de Lutte anti-mines des Nations Unies. cette campagne vise à réduire la circulation illicite des armes et de la violence armée.

data.title: Une proposition de loi prévoit des activités agricoles et des formations professionnelles pour les détenus en RDC
data.description: Une proposition de loi portée par le député Elvis Atsongya Kiyaya est déclarée recevable le vendredi 9 octobre à l’Assemblée nationale prévoit de renforcer la réinsertion socioprofessionnelle des détenus en République démocratique du Congo. Le texte propose notamment des activités agricoles dans les prisons, des formations professionnelles et des mesures destinées à faciliter l’accès à l’emploi après la libération.

data.title: Les combats entre l’AFC/M23 et les Wazalendo provoquent de nouveaux déplacements de civils à Masisi
data.description: Des affrontements entre les combattants de l’AFC/M23 et une coalition de groupes Wazalendo alliés aux FARDC se poursuivent dans plusieurs localités du territoire de Masisi, au Nord-Kivu, provoquant de nouveaux déplacements de civils, selon plusieurs sources concordantes. Des tirs d’armes lourdes et légères ont été entendus depuis l’aube de ce lundi 12 octobre, notamment dans les environs de Rubaya et de Ngungu, après des combats signalés tout au long du week-end.

data.description: Environ 45 personnes ont été tuées dans des affrontements entre les groupes armés CODECO et Convention pour la révolution populaire (CRP), signalés depuis le week-end dans plusieurs localités du territoire de Djugu, en Ituri, rapportent des sources sécuritaires. La situation restait encore tendue le matin de ce lundi 12 octobre, avec des mouvements d’hommes armés signalés à proximité des sites de déplacés de Roe et de Djangi.

data.title: Standards are not Seasonal: What the EC appointments teach both sides
data.description: On Monday, 12 October 2026, President Mahama swore in two new Deputy Chairpersons of the Electoral Commission, Emelia Afi Agbenyo and Dr Joseph Kwaku Asamoah. They fill the vacancies left by Dr Bossman Eric Asare, who resigned with effect from 31 July, and Samuel Tettey, who retired. At the ceremony, the President told them he expected "no preferential treatment" from the Commission for himself, his party or his government.
data.translatedTitle: Standards are not Seasonal: What the EC appointments teach both sides
data.translatedDescription: On Monday, 12 October 2026, President Mahama swore in two new Deputy Chairpersons of the Electoral Commission, Emelia Afi Agbenyo and Dr Joseph Kwaku Asamoah. They fill the vacancies left by Dr Bossman Eric Asare, who resigned with effect from 31 July, and Samuel Tettey, who retired. At the ceremony, the President told them he expected "no preferential treatment" from the Commission for himself, his party or his government.

data.title: Abass Osabutey declares bid for NDC Deputy National Organiser position
data.description:
Abass Mustapha Osabutey, popularly known as “The Capo” in National Democratic Congress (NDC) circles, has declared his intention to contest for the position of Deputy National Organiser of the party.

Mr Osabutey said his nearly two decades of grassroots activism within the NDC had equipped him with the experience needed to contribute to the party’s organisational work ahead of the 2028 general elections.

data.title: THE LAW 101: La Beach Demolitions – The State’s own documents, the courts’ orders – and the bulldozers
data.description:
State power remains when governments and public officials change. The discipline of the rule of law must remain with it.

Because the cost of establishing and respecting legal rights before taking irreversible action may be far less than the cost of defending that action afterwards.

The rule of law is cheaper before the bulldozer than after it.

data.title: Les établissements privés autorisés à suivre l'ancien programme
data.description: Le ministère de l'Éducation nationale fait marche arrière. Quelques mois après l'annonce d'une réforme dans le programme scolaire, il autorise finalement les établissements privés à poursuivre l'application de l'ancien programme scolaire (PS) durant l'année 2026-2027, mais à titre de transition. Un sujet unique sera (…) - Enseignement

data.title: Indígenas brasileños denuncian amenazas de invasión en Amazonía
data.description: Comunidades indígenas de la Amazonía brasileña recibieron audios con amenazas de invasión a sus territorios si Flávio Bolsonaro gana la segunda vuelta presidencial, prevista para el 25 de octubre, según divulgó Folha de S.Paulo. Ocho mensajes de audio obtenidos por el diario advierten sobre una posible ocupación de la tierra indígena Apyterewa, en el estado de Pará, donde habita el pueblo parakanã, y mencionan una eventual victoria del candidato del Partido Liberal. The post Indígenas brasileños denuncian amenazas de invasión en Amazonía first appeared on Cubadebate .

data.title: Continúa atención médica a lesionados por incendio en Manzanillo
data.description: Dos de las cinco personas lesionadas producto del incendio ocurrido anoche en esta ciudad, continúan hoy bajo atención médica especializada en el área de cirugía plástica y caumatología del hospital clínico quirúrgico Celia Sánchez Manduley. La licenciada Mayra de la Paz Garcés, jefa del servicio, informó que ambos permanecen estables y se comunican bien, mientras un equipo multidisciplinario sigue de cerca su evolución, según refiere en Facebook un reporte de la televisora local Golfovision. The post Continúa atención médica a lesionados por incendio en Manzanillo first appeared on Cubadebate .

data.title: Congreso Nacional prorroga hasta diciembre seis amnistías en Honduras
data.description: Tegucigalpa, Honduras. El Congreso Nacional aprobó por unanimidad la prórroga de seis amnistías hasta el 31 de diciembre de 2026, con el propósito de que los hondureños puedan regularizar sus deudas tributarias, municipales y de servicios públicos sin pagar multas, recargos e intereses moratorios contemplados en estos beneficios. La ampliación fue aprobada con dispensa de dos debates, a través de una iniciativa presentada por el diputado nacionalista Antonio Rivera Callejas, ante el vencimiento de las disposiciones previsto para este 12 de octubre. Los beneficios comprenden las áreas tributaria, municipal, vehicular, aportaciones al Instituto Hondureño de Seguridad Social (IHSS) , agua potable y saneamiento, y energía eléctrica. La medida permitirá a personas naturales, empresas y patronos ponerse al día con sus obligaciones pendientes, siempre que cumplan las condiciones de pago establecidas para cada amnistía. Sin embargo, la prórroga no elimina las deudas principales, sino que exime los cargos adicionales contemplados en la normativa. En el caso de la amnistía tributaria, los contribuyentes podrán regularizar sus obligaciones ante el Servicio de Administración de Rentas (SAR) , mientras que los propietarios de vehículos tendrán más tiempo para ponerse al día con los pagos administrados por el Instituto de la Propiedad (IP). Asimismo, los patronos podrán gestionar sus deudas con el IHSS y los usuarios regularizar sus saldos pendientes por agua potable, saneamiento y consumo de energía eléctrica, mediante los pagos o convenios permitidos. El decreto también establece que las instituciones responsables deberán presentar al Congreso Nacional un informe sobre los resultados de las amnistías dentro de los 60 días posteriores a su finalización. Con esta ampliación, los beneficiarios dispondrán de más de dos meses adicionales para regularizar sus obligaciones antes de la fecha límite del 31 de diciembre de 2026.

data.title: Buscan a otros tres implicados en el crimen de Marvin Fernández
data.description: San Pedro Sula, Honduras. Las autoridades policiales tienen en la mira a otros tres implicados en el asesinato del estudiante de Derecho Marvin Omar Fernández . Informaron que las investigaciones apuntan a la participación de dos supuestos autores intelectuales del crimen. También tienen perfilado a un presunto cómplice del sicario que le dio muerte a Fernández y que lo habría ayudado a huir. Por la muerte violenta del pasante de Derecho está en prisión Carlos Eduardo Zaldívar Cervantes , alias Texas, señalado como el sicario que disparó contra Fernández. El sospechoso fue capturado tres días después del asesinato. El Texas tiene auto de formal procesamiento con prisión preventiva, y la audiencia preliminar en el proceso penal que se le sigue está programada para el 24 de noviembre de 2026. Marvin Omar Fernández fue ultimado el 11 de agosto de 2026 dentro del bufete de su esposa, quien es abogada. El despacho está ubicado en la 6 avenida, entre la 4 y la 5 calles suroeste del barrio El Centro. En el proceso contra Zaldívar Cervantes, las autoridades del Ministerio Público (MP) acreditaron las declaraciones de dos testigos presenciales, un reconocimiento en rueda en el que los testigos identificaron al imputado y cuatro pruebas documentales. Además, el MP presentó videos de seguimiento que muestran todo el recorrido de Zaldívar desde el lugar de los hechos hasta la Gran Central Metropolitana , donde lo aguardaba un individuo en un vehículo tipo turismo. En ese automóvil huyó hacia Olanchito, Yoro, donde fue capturado. Las filmaciones muestran el momento en que el sicario ingresa al despacho y se acerca a Fernández. El individuo sacó una pistola que llevaba dentro de una mochila y posteriormente le disparó. El hombre salió del bufete y huyó por la 5.ª avenida en dirección al sur, hasta llegar a la Gran Central Metropolitana. En un inicio, las autoridades policiales manejaron la hipótesis de que Fernández habría sido asesinado por confusión con otro abogado que tenía su bufete en el mismo edificio. Sin embargo, a medida que avanzaron las investigaciones, esa hipótesis perdió fuerza debido a la aparición de nuevos indicios que apuntan a un posible conflicto relacionado con la venta de terrenos. La víctima trabajaba en asuntos legales vinculados a esas propiedades. Las pesquisas de la Policía establecen que Marvin Omar habría recibido amenazas de muerte antes del crimen. Según las averiguaciones, en los mensajes le exigían que devolviera el dinero que le habían pagado por un proceso relacionado con la compra y venta de los terrenos. Fernández trabajaba en ese caso para intentar solucionar los inconvenientes legales que habían surgido en torno a la negociación.
